entities.name: Green Party of the United States
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Green Party of the United States (GPUS), founded 2001 as a national federation of state Green parties (the oldest of which date to 1984), is America's most significant third party of the left — achieving national prominence through Ralph Nader's 2000 presidential campaign (2.74%, 2.88 million votes) that many Democrats blame for Al Gore's Florida defeat and George W. Bush's election, making the Greens the most consequential spoiler party in American electoral history. Nader's 97,421 votes in Florida (Bush won by 537) remains the most debated third-party vote in US history.

The Green Party emerged from the Green movement (environmental politics, Four Pillars: ecology, social justice, grassroots democracy, nonviolence) brought to the US from German Grünen influence. State Green parties formed from the 1980s; Nader ran as Green presidential candidate in 1996 (0.71%) and 2000 (2.74%). The 2000 election controversy made the Greens politically radioactive to many left-leaning voters: 'lesser-evil' voting became the dominant strategy for progressives, suppressing Green support for 20 years.

Jill Stein ran as Green presidential candidate in 2012 (0.36%) and 2016 (1.07%, 1.46 million votes) — with her 51,463 Wisconsin votes exceeding Trump's 22,748 margin again raising the spoiler debate. The Green Party's Four Pillars platform (ecology, social justice, grassroots democracy, nonviolence) and Green New Deal proposal preceded and influenced the Democratic Party's own Green New Deal (2019) championed by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Green Party of the United States — through Nader's 97,421 Florida votes in 2000 that almost certainly cost Al Gore the presidency — is the most consequential spoiler party in American electoral history, with downstream effects on climate policy (Bush's rejection of Kyoto), the Iraq War, and two decades of US political development.
